analysis.one_liner: Restricts and caps attorney fees the federal government must pay people who win cases against it.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2026 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no further action; it has two cosponsors and no votes.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, under the Equal Access to Justice Act, an individual, small business, or nonprofit that beats the federal government in an agency case or a lawsuit can make the government pay its attorney fees, as long as the government's position wasn't substantially justified. This bill would shrink that right in several ways: it would limit fee awards to people with a direct financial stake in the case, cap fees at $200,000 per case and three cases per year, make judges cut awards when lawyers did pro bono work, and ban attorney fees in settlements that force an agency to write a rule or issue guidance. Social Security and Veterans Affairs cases are carved out of the caps.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill passed, the federal government would save money by paying fewer and smaller fee awards. Industries that prefer fewer citizen lawsuits against agencies, and fewer court-enforced settlements that push agencies to regulate, would also benefit. People who currently use fee-shifting to make challenges affordable would lose that protection, except in Social Security and veterans cases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The federal government and regulated industries

how_it_helps.text: The bill caps fee awards against the government at $200,000 per case and three cases per calendar year, unless the case is a class action or involves Social Security or Veterans Affairs [S2].

It would deny fee awards to any party without a direct personal monetary interest, such as a person with an injury, property damage, or an unpaid government payment, screening out advocacy organizations suing on broader public grounds [S2].

It would bar any settlement or consent decree that produces a regulation or guidance document from including payment of attorney fees or litigation costs, removing a tool courts have used to make agencies follow through on commitments [S2].
It would require judges to reduce or deny fee awards commensurate with pro bono hours, and to reduce awards when a party prolonged or misrepresented the case or acted in bad faith [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people and small entities that sue the federal government would bear the cost: attorney fees in a case against the government can easily exceed $200,000, so a capped award leaves the winner paying the difference out of pocket. Public-interest law firms and advocacy groups would lose the fee income that funds their casework, and some cases would become impossible to bring at all.
analysis.who_pays_short: Citizens and groups that sue the government

drawbacks.text: A $200,000 cap can fall far short of actual legal costs in a complex case against the federal government, meaning a prevailing party wins the case but still owes its own lawyers [S2].

Screening out plaintiffs without a direct personal monetary interest would exclude organizations bringing cases on behalf of the public, such as challenges to agency rulemaking, which are often the only check on illegal or arbitrary government action [S2].

Requiring judges to cut awards based on pro bono hours penalizes lawyers for doing free work and makes it harder to assemble representation for people who could not otherwise afford to sue the government [S2].

The strongest good-faith argument for the bill: fee-shifting has been used by repeat litigants and by groups that negotiate consent decrees to make agencies issue rules through backroom settlements rather than public rulemaking, and taxpayers foot the fees. The bill addresses those concerns, but the same provisions would also price ordinary people out of legitimate cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The taxpayer savings are real but modest, and they come at the price of the main mechanism that lets individuals and small businesses afford to challenge the federal government. The carve-outs for Social Security and veterans cases acknowledge how important fee recovery is to ordinary claimants, which underscores what the caps would take away from everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee when it was introduced, and the committee has not acted on it since.

narrative.text: Representative Thomas Tiffany introduced the bill on June 30, 2026, for himself and Representative Harriet Hageman, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S2][S4].
Two Republicans are listed as cosponsors, and no further action, hearing, markup, or vote appears in the bill's history [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one's position has changed yet: the federal government still pays fees under the current rules, and the people and groups that rely on fee-shifting still have it. The bill's supporters have gained nothing so far either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No change yet — current fee rules stand

sides.party_line_note: The bill's three supporters are all Republicans; no Democrat has cosponsored and no opposition has yet been recorded, since the bill has not moved past its referral.

industries.note: The government would pay fewer and smaller fee awards to parties that beat it in court. Its savings come directly out of the ability of individuals and small businesses to afford challenges to government action.

industries.industry: Public-interest law firms and environmental advocacy groups
industries.note: Fee-shifting under the Equal Access to Justice Act funds much of the casework of groups that challenge agency decisions, and the monetary-interest requirement and caps would cut them out. When their lawsuits succeed, the public usually gains the remedy; their loss is the public's loss of that enforcement channel.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (timber, mining, energy and other permit holders)
industries.note: Fewer suits and no fees in settlement agreements mean less legal pressure on agencies to write or enforce rules affecting these industries. The bill's own impact assessment centers on federal forest and rangeland management, where such litigation is concentrated.

industries.industry: Social Security and veterans disability claimants
industries.note: The bill exempts Social Security and Veterans Affairs cases from its caps and monetary-interest test, preserving the largest volume of fee awards that go to ordinary claimants — while other agency cases lose that protection.

analysis.trajectory: A bill referred to committee with only two cosponsors and no scheduled hearing or markup rarely reaches the floor. With the 119th Congress ending January 3, 2027, this bill would need the Judiciary Committee to act quickly, and there is no sign of that; the most likely path is that it dies in committee at the end of the session.
